comment: Known appliances and the LCDproc driver that lights their built-in panel.
Same shape and the same discipline as os-linkhealth's chassis.json: match on SMBIOS, propose
a driver and its options, and say plainly how far the proposal has actually been proven. An
entry is a claim about a machine we cannot see, so every one of them carries a 'confirmed'
line written by whoever watched the screen light up - or left empty, which means nobody has.
Nothing here is applied on its own. The settings page offers the match as a starting point and
the owner presses Apply. A wrong driver writing to the wrong serial port is not a mistake a
plugin should make on its own initiative, and a serial port on an unknown appliance may be
somebody's console.
Matching uses kenv smbios values, exactly as os-linkhealth does. maker/product/version are
regular expressions. The first entry whose every stated field matches wins; 'generic' is the
fallback and proposes nothing at all.
The 'drivers' table below is only a fallback. config.py prefers /usr/local/etc/LCDd.conf.sample,
which the lcdproc package installs and which lists, section by section, every option each
driver really understands. Reading the installed package beats trusting a table copied into
this file, which would rot the first time LCDproc gained an option.

sophos-xg-3xx.confirmed: XG 330 rev 2 (smbios version 330r2), 2026-09-21: the display is verified - LCDd initialised the panel with no errors and the owner photographed live CPU, memory and uptime screens on it. The keypad is verified too: all four keys reported, measured one button at a time at ReportLevel 5 with the screen held still, three presses and three events each. The map above is that measurement and not LCDproc's default order, which puts Enter on 4,1 - where this panel has its down arrow.
notes: ConnectionType=ezio fixes the line at 2400 baud by itself - the driver reported 'serial: using speed: 2400' with no Speed option set, so this entry deliberately does not write one.
Heartbeat must stay off. This panel has no programmable character for LCDproc's heartbeat glyph and draws it as a solid black block in the corner.
DelayMult=2 is what the owner settled on after trying 4: faster, and with RefreshDisplay redrawing the whole screen every few seconds it has not dropped a character.
The panel is printed with a down arrow, ESC, an up arrow and ENTER, in that order, and that is the order of the matrix positions above.

At 2400 baud the display and the keypad share the line: with screens changing every 3 seconds and a full redraw every 4, two thirds of the presses were lost. A quiet screen is what makes this keypad reliable: hold the screen still while measuring the keys, and keep the redraw interval wide on a panel whose keys are used.

sophos-xgs-17.display: Sophos XGS front panel (the XGS 3300: SMBIOS XGS, board 17 / system 3300r1)
comment: Same panel family as the XG 330 entry above - an EZIO serial bridge, the HD44780 command set
behind an 0xFE escape, on /dev/cuau1 - but NOT the same line rate, and that difference is the
whole reason this entry exists. Matched on the SMBIOS version as well as the product, so it
claims only the identity it was confirmed on.
sophos-xgs-17.confirmed: XGS 3300 (smbios XGS, version 17), 2026-10-02: the display is verified at 9600 - LCDd with hd44780, ConnectionType=ezio and Speed=9600 drew two lines of text the owner read on the panel as correct. The keys were measured on 2026-10-17: the owner pressed Enter, Esc, up and down in turn and the bridge sent A, B, C and D, one byte per press, without being asked. Size: 20 columns by 2 lines - the owner set 20x2 on the settings page on 2026-10-13 and the panel paints it, and the GIFAR bridge on this board drives a 20x2 HD44780 (os-xgs-npu's hardware page); the entry had said 16x2, the XG 330's size, until then.
notes: Speed=9600 is required. ConnectionType=ezio on its own fixes the line at 2400, which is right for the XG 330 rev 2 and wrong here: at 2400 this panel draws scattered x-with-a-bar characters - HD44780 code 0xF8 - which is the signature of bytes arriving at a quarter of the receiver's rate. A long start bit fills the low three bits with zeros and the next long bit fills the rest with ones.

The vendor's own daemon sets the port with `stty ispeed 2400`. That sets only the INPUT speed, and a 16550-class UART has a single divisor, so on the vendor's system the line stays at the 9600 default. Reading the vendor's line setting literally is what kept this panel garbled for a week.

A rate sweep that sets the speed on the .init device and then writes through a fresh open of the port is not a reliable way to test this - that method is how every candidate rate once looked wrong. LCDd opens the port once and sets it with tcsetattr, which is why the decisive test was LCDd itself with Speed set.
Heartbeat stays off, as on the XG 330: the panel has no programmable character for it.

The keys are not read by LCDd here. The bridge never answers LCDd's key request (FE 06) and sends a letter of its own accord instead, which LCDd would discard - so LCDd is told Keypad=no and the plugin reads the port itself.

The panel is not drawn by LCDd either. Its bridge carries out no positioning command at all - clear, home and the line addresses are swallowed and do nothing - and writes every character at a cursor that runs round all forty cells, the first row and then the second. LCDd rewrites only what changed, so each update moved the whole picture by however many characters it wrote. The plugin draws this panel itself, always forty characters at once, which leaves the cursor where it was; the owner lines the text up once from the Buttons tab.

sophos-xgs-amda0202.display: Sophos XGS front panel (the XGS 2100, 2300 and 3100: the XGS 3300's board, AMDA0202)
comment: The XGS 3300's entry above, offered to the other models built on its board - AMDA0202, the assembly
number SMBIOS type 2 carries in its serial: the 2100 and 2300 (-0001 and -0002, the two assemblies
the vendor's 1US startup script in its GPL sources names) and the 3100 (-0003, its owner's support
bundle, issue 901). Matched on the board, not on model strings nobody here has read, and offered
unconfirmed: the panel is confirmed on the 3300 alone, which still matches the entry above on its
own strings first.
The text starts at offset 24: the XGS 3100's owner brought the ruler up at offset 0 and read G,
its seventeenth character, in the top left corner (issue 901) - 0 - 16, round forty cells, is 24.
One appliance's reading, offered as the start: bridge.py writes it only where nobody has lined
the text up yet, and Align the text still sets it.
notes: Speed=9600 is required. Text starts at offset 24: an XGS 3100's ruler came up with its G in the top left corner (os-xgs-npu issue 901). If the text sits elsewhere on yours, Align the text, on the Buttons tab, sets it.
sophos-xgs-amda0202.hint: Proposed from the board: these models are built on the XGS 3300's board, AMDA0202, on which this panel was confirmed at 9600, and an XGS 3100's owner saw the 2400 signature - scattered x-with-a-bar characters - under the general entry. Press Test after applying: two lines of text read right on the panel confirm it.

sophos-xgs-family.display: Sophos XGS (panel not confirmed on this model)
comment: A Sophos XGS whose model nobody has watched here, ahead of the general entry below for one
thing: the size. The XGS panels seen so far - the 3300's and a 3100's, one board - are 20
characters by 2 lines, and the general entry's 16x2 is the older XG panels' size: an XGS 3100
owner's settings came from it at 16x2 (issue 901). Everything else is the general entry's,
and offered as a guess the same way.
sophos-xgs-family.hint: Nobody has confirmed this model yet. XGS panels confirmed so far - on an XGS 3300 and an XGS 3100 - are 20 characters by 2 lines, so 20x2 is proposed here; older XG models keep 16x2. Press Test after applying: two lines of text read right on the panel confirm it. The key map is copied from XG 330 rev 2 and is a guess here: measure it with the key test before you trust which button is which.

sophos-xg-family.display: Sophos XG / XGS (panel not confirmed on this model)
comment: A Sophos box whose exact model we have not watched. The hardware is close enough that the
same proposal is worth offering, but it is offered as a guess and labelled as one: the
settings page shows the empty 'confirmed' line and says nobody has seen this work yet.
sophos-xg-family.hint: Nobody has confirmed this model yet. Press Test after applying: if the panel stays dark, try the driver list - mtc_s16209x lights a screen of this shape and cannot read a button, which is the honest fallback. The key map is copied from the XG 330 rev 2 and is a guess here: measure it with the key test before you trust which button is which.

generic.hint: No proposal for this machine. Choose a driver and a serial port by hand - the page lists the drivers this installation of LCDproc actually carries and the ports this machine actually has - then press Test. Sending a report of what worked is how this table grows.

comment: Fallback only, used when /usr/local/etc/LCDd.conf.sample is missing. Every option name here
was read out of that sample on the reference machine (lcdproc 0.5.9_1), not remembered.
A driver absent from this table is not refused: config.py writes what the panel entry asks
for and says in its answer that it could not check the option names.
Where each adjustable speed from the settings page lands in LCDd.conf. The three server
options exist whatever the driver is. The two driver options do not: DelayMult belongs to
hd44780 and sed1520 only, RefreshDisplay to hd44780 only, and writing either into a section
that has never heard of it makes LCDd complain on every start. config.py checks the driver's
real option list before writing them, and reports the knobs it had to leave out.
